Manuscript Title: Diverse clonal fates emerge upon drug treatment of homogeneous cancer 
cells 
Reviewer Comments & Author Rebuttals 
Reviewer Reports on the Initial Version: 
Referees' comments: 
 
Referee #1 (Remarks to the Author): 
 
This is an interesting and important paper focused on the crucial question of exploring how cell and 
clonal composition are shaped by intrinsic and extrinsic factors. To this end, the authors combine an 
expressed barcode library with a “sister replicates” concept to elegantly distinguish between 
different possibilities that may explain the diverse phenotypes associated with resistance to targeted 
therapy observed in their system under treatment. Through a series of experiments and 
computational analyses, the authors conclude that there is a high transcriptional and phenotypic 
variability in cancer cell lines, that this variation is “predetermined” by molecular differences 
between cells before drug treatment (rather than extrinsic factors), and is impacted by dose and 
type of drug. 
 
The topic is timely and important and the study is very extensive. There are many elegant and clever 
aspects of the study. For example, using the “identical twin” analysis to reveal effects of neighboring 
cells is a very clever idea. However, we have two over-arching concerns that must be addressed to 
fully support the conclusions of the study. Those would need to be addressed and shown in a 
revision. 
 
First, this concept of diverse resistance states has been explored extensively by multiple studies labs 
and there is a crucial need in this study to show data for the initial degree of homogeneity or 
variation of the population in light of these earlier studies. In particular, Ben David et al., 2017, 
showed that variation in gene expression arises de novo, in addition to reflecting selection of pre-
existing subclones over a relatively short time course of culturing. Moreover, multiple other studies 
have showed that cell line cancer models display significant transcriptional and functional 
heterogeneity (Kuiken et al., 2021, Naffar-Abu Amara et al., 2020, Khan et al., 2017, Meir et al., 
2020, Kinker et al., 2020 to name of few). While some of these studies relied on single cell cloning 
and done at a smaller scale compared to the reviewed study, they provide a more in-depth 
characterization of the different clones as well as a mechanistic links to what underlies the observed 
diversity. For instance, the cell line HMLER is known to harbor both epithelial and mesenchymal cells 
and much work has been done to try to address this intra cell line heterogeneity and how it relates 
to tumorigenicity (for example Kroger et al., 2019). Most importantly, these studies showed that 
even following single cell cloning one can detect genetic changes and that some of them can 
accumulate over a mere couple of passages. As such, the authors description of the population of 
cells in the manuscript as “homogenous” is a strong assumption that raises concerns. The authors 
did not perform any single cell genome sequencing analysis to show that there are no mutations and

thus such uniformity in genomic space cannot be assumed based on their experimental design. This 
needs to be directly addressed to draw the necessary conclusions. 
 
Second, on the computational side, we did feel that the authors could have performed a more 
careful analysis in several important places and shown robustness of the conclusions to specific 
analytical choices. In particular, the approach the authors used is heavily dependent on initial 
clustering and it is critical to see that the conclusions are not sensitive to this particular choice, and 
would hold when using a statistical framework that does not rely on hard partitioning, especially as 
gene expression does not always obey such boundaries. 
 
We elaborate on these points and other specific comments below, in an order that follows their 
appearance in the paper. 
 
Major comments 
 
1. While the authors claim the initial culture is “homogeneous” because of the single cell cloning 
process, we could not find an estimate of how any cell divisions/time passed from the single cell 
clone to the initial culture. Moreover, as noted above, we feel strongly that the authors should 
include some genomics (DNA) analysis of the cell lines. 
 
2. The authors state “we found extensive diversity in their gene expression profiles”. To make this 
statement, the authors should compare to the diversity to the untreated cell line. 
 
3. Figure 1. There are clearly two major clusters and a couple of minor ones, but the authors work at 
much finer granularity, and it is a bit less clear how to interpret the smaller subclusters and their 
relation to known mechanisms of resistance in melanoma. Moreover, as we note above, some of the 
finer patterns may not be best captured by clustering. 
 
4. How large was the initial barcoded parental population? This was not clear from the supplement. 
A single 6-well plate with 100K cell per well? Or just a single well? If it was 600K cells why is 
transduction 3 lower? (Supplementary Figure 1C). 
 
5. “It is worth noting that these cells might normally be missed in conventional analysis”. Why? In 
our reasoning, the authors didn’t enrich for these cells, and therefore we would expect them to be 
present in other studies as well. Based on visual inspection, it seems like singletons are a non-
negligible percent of the dataset. 
 
6. The assessment of transcriptional homogeneity by assignment to cluster appears as an 
inappropriate statistical framework for us. The authors analysis is more geared to answer: are the 
clones enriched in specific clusters, but the question they are asking is about homogeneity and 
clusters can have plenty of internal variation too. We ask that the authors modify the framework 
they use to assess the degree of expression homogeneity directly. 
 
7. The association of transcription state/cluster with clone size (Figure 2B) requires more formal 
statistical analysis. Ideally, there would also be some validation -- either by direct experiments or by

reference to other studies 
 
8. Is the restricted transcriptional space at the clone level (Figure 3) also observed without 
treatment? 
 
9. Is the mouse treatment (PLX4720) different than what is used in the rest of the study? If so, why? 
 
10. Comparing Figures 4B and E, in vivo and in vitro look very different. We are thus not sure this 
supports the paragraph claim and the authors should reconsider the conclusion. 
 
11. From Supplementary Figure 4H, the authors claim that the “three largest clones appeared to 
occupy similar transcriptional states”. Could this merely be because they are all proliferating cells, 
and the cell cycle dominates the signal? 
 
11. In Supplementary Figure 4E, the authors report a high silencing rate and an overall lower 
barcode detection rate compared to other recent studies that have used an expressed barcode 
library (such as Weinreb et al., 2020, Oren et al., 2021). Therefore, it is very important that the 
authors test how such a high fraction of missing data affects the inference and both clone size and 
clonal presence/absence analysis. 
 
Minor comments 
1. Figure 1D. Please label the subpanels or refer to it later in the text, as it was confusing to follow. 
 
2. Please include a plot that shows the number of barcodes per cell and the number of cells with 
assigned barcode per sample. 
 
3. Please include a plot that shows what was the distribution of the clone size per sample and how 
many were singletons. Would be good to also mention what is the fraction of the largest clone. 
 
4. What is the difference between Supplementary Fig 1H and Figure 2B? 
 
5. “new clones survive the low dose and reprogram to become”. Please revise and do not use the 
term “reprogram” as there is no comparison to the clone’s naïve state 
 
6. In Figure 6: Vemurafenib as at 1uM and trametinib at 5nM. How were these doses chosen? 
 
7. For neighbors analysis “the number of neighbors… to be a minimum of 10 and the size of the 
smaller of the two…” did you mean or? 
 
8. “For the computational analysis of barcoded single cell datasets”- a Levenshtein distance of <=8 
appears to us as a high threshold. How sensitive are the results to this choice?

Referee #2 (Remarks to the Author): 
 
In this study, Goyal et al., combine DNA barcoding with single-cell RNA-seq to track the fates of 
cancer cells exposed to a range of anti-cancer therapies. Using this high-resolution method, the 
authors showed that resistant clones occupy a distinct array of functional and molecular fates. An 
elegant experimental strategy to split sisters across different experimental groups demonstrated 
that the different resistant cell fates are predetermined by molecular differences that exist in the 
cells prior to drug addition (rather than extrinsic factors guiding the resistant fate choice). By varying 
drug dose and type, the authors were able to manipulate fate outcomes in the resistant clones. 
Altogether, this is an extremely well-communicated and elegantly designed study. Further, 
considering the insight that this work provides into resistance dynamics, the findings are significant. 
 
Major comments: 
 
- I have few technical concerns with this study, and most of my comments can be addressed via 
analysis of the existing data. However – and this comes with an acknowledgment that what I raise is 
technically challenging/out of scope – I was hoping that the authors would at least discuss the 
concept of state-fate analysis. For example, in the discussion, the authors state, “These outcomes 
are largely predetermined by molecular differences in the initial state of cells, some of which have 
been elucidated” sets the stage for further exploration of what these molecular differences might 
be, yet this isn’t expanded on. 
 
- My main technical concern centers on the conclusion that “the emergence of cell fate diversity 
upon treatment of single-cell-derived cancer cell lines may be universal”, based on analysis of the 
breast cancer cell line behavior. This conclusion is not well-supported by the data (for example, 
there is no statistical test for Supplementary Figure 4H to support this conclusion) and may well be 
confounded by the observed silencing. 
 
- I appreciate the demonstration of silencing in the above breast cancer cell line. It would be ideal to 
show the same kind of silencing analysis in the melanoma cell line. For example, does the singleton 
population demonstrate any differences in silencing relative to the expanding population? 
 
- Genes differentially expressed between morphology types from bulk RNA sequencing were 
identified and used to map morphologies to single-cell clusters from Fatemap. This is a very neat 
analysis. Could all major clusters in the scRNA-seq data be accounted for using this method? If not, 
does it suggest that some morphology classes have been overlooked? 
 
- For Figures 1H and 3, further quantification of the imaging will complement the scRNA-seq data 
demonstrating consistent clonal gene expression. 
 
- The ‘mixing coefficient’ metric for transcriptional similarity is very elegant, as is the design of the 
low/high drug dose experiments. For the non-expert, the authors have done an excellent job of 
communicating the experimental design and potential interpretation of outcomes.

Referee #3 (Remarks to the Author): 
 
The manuscript from the lab of Arjun Raj and colleagues focuses upon the trajectories of drug 
resistance in melanoma cells. They specifically ask whether patterns of resistance are pre-
determined and if different drugs impact the heterogeneity of the resistant cells that emerge. As 
their approach, the investigators use a novel method of bar coding paired with single cell RNA-
sequencing to track to the fates of individual cells. Strengths of the study include the innovative 
methodology and the conceptually interesting idea that resistance phenotypes are pre-determined. 
Weaknesses of the study include the limited range of cell lines used, questions about the 
translational nature of the findings (these are mostly cell culture experiments with established cell 
lines) and the lack of consideration of how the immune system would shape the responses that the 
authors observe. In addition, quite a few broad sweeping statements are made that are not directly 
supported by the data. 
 
General points 
 
The observations that cancer cells can adopt a range of pre-specified fates upon drug exposure is 
interesting and worthy of investigation. From a more philosophical point of view, have the authors 
considered whether this large range of phenotypes is unique to cancer cells, can normal cells do 
similar things? Does the mutational background of the cancer cell pre-specify what the potential 
transcriptional programs would be? In the current study two melanoma cell lines (and one breast 
cancer cell line) were profiled and although there was some agreement in 
phenotypic/transcriptional behavior, I wonder how the range of resistant cell states observed was 
influenced by genotype? For example, would one expect to see the same range of phenotypes from 
melanoma cells that are N-ras mutant, or maybe even triple wild-type? If similar phenotypes are 
seen, one could reason that the range of phenotypes available to the melanoma cells are more likely 
to be lineage-specific rather than a consequence of the mutational landscape. I am not sure that 
these questions are easily answered, but I think they are worth considering as part of the overall 
concept being advanced here. 
 
Specific points 
 
1. There is strong evidence that observations about heterogeneity in in vitro or preclinical studies 
differ from what is observed in melanoma patients. What evidence is there that the observations 
made in the paper are of any clinical relevance? Is there any clinical validation of the central 
hypothesis, in say matched pre and post-BRAF inhibitor treated samples? Most of the observations 
in the present manuscript are from studies of established cell lines adapted to cell culture and grown 
in vitro. Studies in short-term cultures from patients e.g. within 1-2 passages of establishment would 
be more relevant. Direct clinical evidence would be even better. 
2. In the abstract it is stated that the resistant states were not dictated by external environmental 
influences. I am not sure that this was directly tested in this study. Most of the experiments were 
performed under cell culture conditions, and the potential influence of things like hypoxia, stromal 
contact, immune infiltration, nutrient availability, mechanical stress etc was never investigated. I 
think the statement should be qualified because as written it’s a bit misleading. 
3. The observation that single cancer cells can give rise to diverse states is interesting, and argues

against prior suggestions that resistance emerges from pre-existing clonal populations that just 
expand under therapy. One question is what defines the pre-existing epigenetic landscape that 
allows so many diverse transcriptional states to emerge? Is this plastic epigenetic state determined 
by the mutational burden of the tumor (e.g. mutations in epigenetic regulators) or is it a lineage-
specific malleable epigenetic state? 
4. A further question is how different are the resistant states from each other? From the UMAP 
representation there seems to be two major clusters. The authors have differentiated these further, 
but I wonder how much overlap there is between the sub-states in the two major clusters. Are these 
statistically different? The phenotypic data helps address this a little, but it might be helpful to more 
formally quantify these differences. 
5. Some of the cell state gene signatures seem to be more immune based. Is it likely that these 
would grow out more (or less?) if the experiment was carried out in vivo in syngeneic mice? Again, 
this comes back to addressing whether environmental factors would help to determine the 
trajectory of resistance. As noted before this is difficult to answer using cell culture models or in 
mouse xenograft studies. 
6. In Figure 2 it is surprising to me that the resistant colonies maintain their phenotypes after being 
expanded. Were these maintained in drug (I don’t believe it was stated in the text). Did the authors 
reprofile these to determine if there was any phenotypic drift following expansion over months? 
7. Figure 3 is very hard to interpret. What it seems to show is limited numbers of cells from selected 
regions of a mouse tumor that express some of the markers identified in Figure 1. It would be more 
meaningful to show lower-power images with some staining for markers for each of the sub-clusters 
(MLANA etc) so the reader could discern whether these genes are just expressed in a few individual 
cells or across entire clonal areas of a tumor. 
8. The mouse experiment in figure 5B does not show a vehicle control. In addition, the anti-tumor 
effects of the vemurafenib seem very weak. Even the high dose does little to control growth. Was 
this the best model to use? It seems like it was intrinsically resistant. A better model may have been 
one in which near complete tumor remission was achieved followed by relapse. 
9. There has been some interest in discontinuous drug dosing in melanoma, which although effective 
in xenograft models often leads to a faster onset of resistance in patients. How would on and off 
cycles of vemurafenib switch the make up of resistant lineages compared to continual dosing? 
10. Was any sequencing of the resistant lineages undertaken to determine if there were genetic 
drivers of resistance preferentially selected for in any of the resistant clones? 
11. What is the mechanism underlying growth arrest vs. survival when low doses vs high doses of 
vemurafenib were used? Is it tied into differential effects on the cell cycle vs apoptosis, do different 
sub-clusters have different sensitivities to cell cycle affects vs. cell death? 
12. The differences between vemurafenib and trametinib are perhaps not that surprising given that 
vemurafenib impacts many other kinases in addition to BRAF. Trametinib in contrast is very specific 
and only impacts MEK. This needs to be discussed in more detail. 
13. The data with the DOTL1 inhibition is intriguing and I am not sure whether the authors have 
already addressed this, but what is the impact of DOTL1 inhibition in the context of vemurafenib 
resistance in vivo? Does depleting the MLANA sub-cluster through DOTL inhibition alter the 
trajectory to resistance in vivo? This should be explored. 
14. Discussion. I think the following statement needs toning down “For instance, we showed that 
treatment with trametinib, a MEK inhibitor, was able to eliminate specific resistant fates that 
otherwise continue to persist in treatment with the canonical drug vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor

(both of which impinge on the same molecular pathway). These differences may help explain the 
effectiveness of newer dual therapy regimens combining both MEK and BRAF inhibition in 
melanoma patients”. I don’t think the subtle alteration of specific fates that the authors observe 
under monotherapy versus combination therapy mechanistically explains the dramatically improved 
clinical responses seen in patients. Clinically, >30% of patients with advanced melanoma have very 
long term responses to the BRAF-MEK inhibitor combination of 5+ years. This is typically associated 
with a complete remission of disease and no resistance. I think it is a stretch to correlate these 
subtle changes in transcriptional heterogeneity to these profound anti-tumor responses.

We thank the reviewer for pointing us to these studies and raising the issue of genetic homogeneity in
general. We agree that this assumption is critical and worth validating experimentally. We have now
conducted a number of whole-genome sequencing studies to quantify the degree of genetic
heterogeneity in cells both before and after becoming resistant.
In order to assess heterogeneity with sufficient quality within single cells, we grew out several individual
clones from the initial untreated and resistant populations, then performed whole genome sequencing
on those (1 parental clone, 8 untreated clones and 16 resistant clones) to determine the mutational
signature in these cells.
Our results demonstrated that there were no significant statistical patterns in our genome sequencing
data that could explain the variety of transcriptional fates we observed. In our first analysis, we looked

melanoma-related genes

of underlying heterogeneity in the population. We think the manuscript has been strengthened
considerably by their addition.
Furthermore, we agree with the reviewer completely that the literature they cite provides critical context
(both genetic and non-genetic) for the field and for our work. We have now included a discussion of
these papers in the discussion section:
Our work joins a burgeoning literature on genetic and non-genetic sources of cellular
heterogeneity in cancer. Cell line profiling has shown surprising levels of variability, even in
clonal lines, perhaps reflecting clonal memory
(Kuiken
et al. 2022; Ben-David et al. 2018; Meir
et al. 2020; Kinker et al. 2020; Shaffer et al. 2020)
.

.

particular, the approach the authors used is heavily dependent on initial clustering and it is critical to see that
the conclusions are not sensitive to this particular choice, and would hold when using a statistical framework
that does not rely on hard partitioning, especially as gene expression does not always obey such boundaries.
The reviewer raises an excellent point about the robustness of our conclusions to the particularities of
the clustering choices we made. For all the analyses involving the use of clusters, we have performed
the analysis with fewer and more clusters (by changing shared nearest-neighbor resolution), and we
arrived at essentially the same conclusions (Supplementary Figure 5C-E).

We also completely agree that in general, clustering is
per se
relatively arbitrary. Hence, most of our
key results, such as the memory preserved between twins and the mixing coefficient
are completely
independent of any clustering
and are instead performed
on distances computed from the underlying
count values themselves. For instance, the mixing coefficient is computed using the distance between
nearest neighbors in the 50-dimensional principal component (PC) space of the underlying RNA counts
and is independent of clustering. We have also expanded the use of mixing coefficients derived from
the PC space to measure clonal restriction in transcriptional space. We have added this point in the
main text:

We reasoned that for randomly sampled barcode clones, the mixing coefficient would be close
to 1 because two randomly sampled clones would have a high likelihood of each being spread
out uniformly throughout the principal component space. In contrast, the mixing coefficient
would be lower than 1 for experimentally observed clones if they each marked different
transcriptional spaces and were not randomly distributed. Our results from this
clustering-independent analysis indeed corroborated our hypothesis that clones were relatively
transcriptionally homogeneous as compared to the overall population (Supplementary Figure
5A).
Throughout the manuscript, we use the UMAPs solely as a visualization tool.
Supplementary Figure 5A.
a. We formulated a quantitative metric, the mixing coefficient, to calculate the transcriptional
relatedness of different clones to each other. For each pair of barcoded clones, we calculated
the nearest neighbors for each cell in the 50-dimensional principal component space. We then
classified the neighbors as “self” if the neighbors are from the same barcode clone or “non-self”
if they belong to another barcode clone. The mixing coefficient is the ratio of the averaged
fraction of self neighbors to the averaged fraction of non-self neighbors. The higher the mixing

contrast, the mixing coefficient would be lower than 1 for experimentally observed clones if they
each marked different transcriptional spaces and were not randomly distributed. Our results
from this clustering-independent analysis indeed corroborated our hypothesis that clones were

In Discussion
FateMap revealed a rich structure of resistant cell states. The level at which particular groupings
of these states reflect phenotypically distinct outcomes remains to be fully worked out. At the
level of groupings highlighted here, we have demonstrated phenotypic differences in
morphology, growth rate and invasibility; however, it is unclear whether there are subclusters
within these groupings that represent further differences in phenotype.
Throughout the manuscript, we use the UMAPs solely as a visualization tool. There are a few instances
in which our analyses were inherently cluster-based (fraction of dominant cluster, for instance), and so
for those, we have performed sensitivity analyses with more or fewer clusters, showing that our
conclusions were unchanged (Supplementary Figure 5).

Supplementary Figure 5A.
a. We formulated a quantitative metric, the mixing coefficient, to calculate the transcriptional
relatedness of different clones to each other. For each pair of barcoded clones, we calculated
the nearest neighbors for each cell in the 50-dimensional principal component space. We then
classified the neighbors as “self” if the neighbors are from the same barcode clone or “non-self”
if they belong to another barcode clone. The mixing coefficient is the ratio of the averaged
fraction of self neighbors to the averaged fraction of non-self neighbors. The higher the mixing
coefficient, the higher the transcriptional relatedness of the barcoded clones analyzed (a value
of 1 corresponds to perfect mixing, and a value of 0 corresponds to no mixing). We reasoned
that for randomly sampled barcode clones, the mixing coefficient will be close to 1 because two
randomly sampled clones will have a high likelihood of each being spread out uniformly
throughout the principal component space. In contrast, the mixing coefficient will be lower than 1
for experimentally observed clones if they each mark different clusters and are not randomly
distributed. We found that this was indeed the case where the mixing coefficient was close to 1
for randomly sampled pseudo-clones, which was much higher than the mixing coefficient for
experimentally observed clones, suggesting that each clone is constrained in the transcriptional
space.
As noted below, we have now performed a suite of further analyses to support our claims. In particular,
we performed an analysis that is independent of clustering or UMAP projections in which we looked at
the average correlation in the transcriptome profile between paired cells within a clone vs. a randomly
selected clone of the same size (Supplementary Figure 6; see also below) (by correlation in the
transcriptome profile, we mean for each pair, what is the correlation coefficient of the expression of all
genes between the two cells). We found these correlations to be significantly stronger for pairs drawn
from experimentally observed clones as compared to pairs from randomly sampled clones, thus
showing that experimentally observed clones are more homogenous than randomly sampled clones,
independently of any particular clustering. This behavior was independent of the clone size or the
number of genes used for the analysis (Supplementary Figure 6A,B). We performed additional analysis
by calculating the Shannon diversity
(Jiang et al.
2022; Fennell et al. 2022)
, which nicely corroborated
our results from gene correlation analysis. Next, we calculated phenotypic volume
(Fennell et al. 2022)
for all clones and clusters, a metric that enables us to compare the homogeneity of clones with those of

clusters themselves. A higher phenotypic volume implies more heterogeneity in the high-dimensional
transcriptional space. We normalized the phenotypic volume to account for different numbers of cells
and found that clones were more homogenous than the Seurat clusters (Supplementary Figure 6D).
Lastly, we trained a support vector machine model
(Mold et al. 2022)
on 80% of cells within
experimentally observed large clones (>100 cells) and corresponding sized randomly shuffled clones.
We reasoned that if the model could predict the remaining 20% of the cells within experimental clones
better than randomized clones, it would suggest that clones are more homogenous within themselves
than the general population. Indeed, we found a much higher accuracy of prediction for testing data
from experimental clones as compared to the shuffled counterparts (Supplementary Figure 6E). This
result was consistent across two biological replicates (Supplementary Figure 6F).

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and suggesting this excellent experiment. In the

compare the properties of resistant lineages between continuous and discontinuous dosing
(Supplementary Figure 23A,B). We found that while there was indeed overlap of resistant lineages

discontinuously dosed arm were particularly enriched in the melanocytic cluster (marked by
MLANA
expression). This was also evident from the comparatively much darker color of the pellet of resistant

dosed arm tended to be proliferative to varying degrees, and belonged predominantly to the
melanocytic cluster although some clones did belong to other clusters (Supplementary Figure 23F).

MLANA

be singletons under continuous dosing, as we saw
previously (Figure 2), we noticed in contrast that the majority (68%) of clones in the MLANA-high cluster
proliferated to form large clones (Supplementary Figure 23G). Furthermore, while the total cells
analyzed for scRNA-seq in each condition were comparable, discontinuous dosing had 3.6-fold more
unique clones than in continuous dosing, suggesting that intermittent removal of drug can enable some
clones, otherwise slated to die in continuous dosing, survive in discontinuous dosing (Supplementary

into a much higher number of resistant cells in discontinuous dosing as compared to continuous dosing
(Supplementary Figure 23C). Lastly, analysis of twins shared across continuous and discontinuous
dosing revealed that while some twins are robust to the dosing regimens, many others tend to switch to
melanocytic fate in discontinuous dosing (Supplementary Figure 23I).

lead to increased therapy resistance, matching what happens in patients, and our results demonstrate

the conceptual possibility that growth of certain resistant fate types may be responsible for this
behavior. We thank the reviewer for suggesting this highly interesting experiment. We have now
updated our main text to describe these results as well:

continuously) has been posed as a means by which to decrease therapy resistant tumor burden

colony sizes was consistent for both the original and the subclone lines (Supplementary Figure
